opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly it's something I went back and forth on over the years.

The way I'd put it is that the research I did, things like the biological anchors report or the work on how we might end up with misaligned AI by default, was always in service of grantmaking, but often quite indirectly. Open Phil's job is to figure out where marginal dollars do the most good. In a lot of cause areas you can lean on an existing field: there are experts, there's an evidence base, and you're mostly trying to find the best people and fund them. With transformative AI, especially back when I started on it, that scaffolding didn't really exist. Nobody had a well-developed answer to basic questions like when this might happen, how fast, or what the main risks would look like. And those answers really matter for how you allocate. If you think powerful AI is fifty years out, you might fund field-building and academic research with long payoff horizons. If you think it could be ten or fifteen years out, you'd want to move much faster and fund different things.

So I saw the worldview investigations work as trying to build the foundation the grantmaking stood on. It was less "here's a grant recommendation" and more "here's our best attempt at a model of the world that our grantmakers and leadership can argue with and plan around."

That said, there was always tension. Those projects took a long time, sometimes much longer than planned, and there's a real question whether a funder should be producing big public research reports versus just making decisions and moving on. I think a lot of the value ended up coming from making our reasoning legible, both internally and to the broader world, so people could poke holes in it. Over time I got more interested in work that was closer to the action, things like thinking concretely about what technical research to fund and what an alignment research agenda should prioritize, partly because I felt the timelines picture had become less of a bottleneck than the "okay, so what do we actually do" question.

r001.rationale: She describes her research as indirectly supporting grantmaking and contrasts it with direct grant recommendations, identifying a gap between the intellectual work and giving grants.

r002.rationale: She says the research projects took a long time and later became more interested in work closer to action, but does not say that her attraction to deeper intellectual projects drew her away from participating in grantmaking.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that they were always pretty tightly coupled, even when it didn't look that way from the outside. When I was at Open Phil, the research I did—the timelines report, the stuff on how training might produce misaligned models—that wasn't a side project I was doing for its own sake. It grew out of the question the organization actually had to answer, which was: how much should we be spending on AI, how urgently, and on what?

So, like, the biological anchors work came out of a very concrete need. Holden and others were trying to figure out whether transformative AI was something to take seriously on a decades timescale or a centuries timescale, and that answer really changes what you do as a funder. If it's centuries, you're mostly doing field-building and maybe you're a little patient. If it's decades, you're in a very different posture. And nobody had done the exercise of actually sitting down and trying to put numbers on it in a way that could be argued with. So the report was, in a sense, an input to a grantmaking strategy, and I think it did actually move the organization's thinking.

But I'd also say the relationship went the other way. Doing grantmaking gives you a kind of ground truth that pure research doesn't. You're talking to the labs, you're talking to academics, you're seeing which proposals come in and which don't, you're seeing what people are confused about. And that shapes which questions feel worth working on. The "training game" stuff, the worry that you'd get models that behave well because they've learned the test rather than because they share your goals—part of why that felt important to write up was that I kept seeing that the people we might fund didn't have a shared crisp picture of the threat model. So writing it down was partly a way of trying to make the grantmaking better by making the field's thinking better.

I'll admit there was always some tension, though. Research at that level of depth takes a long time, and grantmaking has deadlines and budgets and a lot of operational work. There were definitely periods where I felt like I was doing both a bit poorly rather than one well. And I think over time I came to see my comparative advantage as being on the "figure out what's true and explain it clearly" side, and let that feed into decisions other people were making, rather than trying to be the person making all the decisions myself. So I'd say the projects were in service of the grantmaking, but they were also the thing I felt I could uniquely contribute, and those two things mostly pointed in the same direction.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts deep research with grantmaking’s deadlines, budgets, and operational work, describing tension between the two even while saying the research informed grantmaking.

r002.rationale: The response says Cotra’s comparative advantage was research that informed others’ decisions, but does not say attraction to intellectual projects drew her away from participating in grantmaking.

astra-6.text:
I saw those intellectual projects as inputs into grantmaking, even when the connection was pretty indirect. If we’re trying to decide how much to spend on reducing risks from advanced AI, for example, our beliefs about when that technology might arrive matter a lot. They affect both how urgent the work seems and what kinds of work we want to support.

So the aim wasn’t just to pursue an interesting question and arrive at a view. It was to make our assumptions explicit enough that we could ask, “What would we do differently if this were true?” There’s still a substantial gap between a broad research conclusion and deciding whether a particular grant is good. But I thought of the research as helping set the strategy within which those individual decisions get made.

r001.rationale: The response says the intellectual projects informed grantmaking strategy and notes a gap between research conclusions and individual grant decisions. It does not identify a mismatch between Cotra’s abstract work and Open Philanthropy’s core activity of giving money.

sol-6.1.text:
I saw those intellectual projects as inputs into grantmaking. A lot of the questions we were trying to answer—when might very powerful AI arrive, how much should we prioritize it, and what kinds of work could help—were questions where your answer could really change how you allocate resources.

So the point wasn’t necessarily that each research project would identify a particular grant to make. It was more about building a framework for deciding how much to spend in an area, how urgently to spend it, and what assumptions our strategy depended on. There’s a pretty long chain between a big-picture research question and an individual grant, but I saw that as part of the core work, rather than a separate intellectual pursuit.

r001.rationale: The response describes a long chain between abstract research questions and individual grants, distinguishing the intellectual work from direct grantmaking.
